question:
Patient note:
A 37-year-old man was evaluated this afternoon in the ambulatory orthopedic suite in preparation for an urgent right knee arthroscopy that is scheduled for first case tomorrow morning. Three weeks ago he slipped on an icy sidewalk and sustained a nondisplaced tibial plateau fracture confirmed on CT; because the articular step-off was minimal he was managed non-operatively with a long-leg fiberglass cast that extends from the high thigh to the ankle and was instructed to remain strictly non-weight-bearing. Since the injury he reports spending nearly all day reclining in bed with his right leg elevated on pillows, getting up only for hygiene and meals with axillary crutches. He describes constant dull ache around the fracture site and occasional muscle spasms but denies shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough, fevers, chills, night sweats, abdominal pain, or change in bowel habits. There has been no recent hospitalization, bloodstream infection, or respiratory illness. His medical history is otherwise notable only for a thrombotic episode five years ago: after a trans-Atlantic flight he developed pain and tightness in the left calf, and duplex ultrasonography revealed an occlusive clot in the popliteal vein. He completed a six-month course of warfarin at that time with complete symptom resolution and has had no recurrence. He has never experienced clot migration to the lungs, never required tunneled catheters or ports, and is unaware of any relatives with abnormal clotting tendencies. He does not have chronic cardiac disease, chronic lung disease, inflammatory bowel conditions, active or prior cancer, myocardial infarction, or varicosities of the lower extremities. He takes no prescribed medicines other than acetaminophen-codeine every six hours for pain and over-the-counter vitamin D, and he has avoided non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs at the surgeon’s request. He does not smoke, drinks beer socially on weekends, and denies illicit substance use. Surgical history is limited to an uncomplicated appendectomy at age 20. Review of systems is otherwise negative. On physical examination he is lying supine on the stretcher, appears comfortable, and converses easily. Vital signs: blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats/min, regular; respiratory rate 14/min; temperature 36.7 °C; oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. Cardiovascular exam reveals normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with equal air entry. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender, with normoactive bowel sounds. The right lower limb is encased in an intact cast; the toes are warm with brisk capillary refill, distal dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable, and there is no apparent swelling beyond expected postoperative-appearing fullness at the fracture site. The left leg is uncovered and symmetric without pitting edema, skin discoloration, or tenderness along the calf veins. Homans sign is absent. There are no superficial dilated veins on either side. Neurologic exam shows intact sensation in the plantar and dorsal aspects of both feet, and motor testing of the left side is full; motor strength of the right side cannot be assessed because of immobilization. Skin elsewhere is intact with no pressure injuries. Baseline laboratory studies obtained today reveal hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, platelet count 246 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 7.3 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, glucose 98 mg/dL, and a normal coagulation profile (prothrombin time 12.6 s, INR 1.0, aPTT 30 s). Chest radiograph is clear, and a 12-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. The anesthesia team documented an airway grade of Mallampati I and no anticipated intubation difficulty. Orthopedic surgery plans to perform diagnostic arthroscopy with possible meniscal shaving and microfracture, expecting a tourniquet time of less than 90 minutes. No chemical or mechanical venous prophylaxis has yet been initiated, and the patient remains n.p.o. after midnight pending the procedure.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score adds weighted risk factors for perioperative venous thromboembolism.
- Age 37 (under 41): 0 points.
- Tibial plateau fracture three weeks ago: a leg fracture within one month scores 5 points.
- Immobilizing long-leg cast: 2 points.
- Mobility: counting his near-continuous reclining as current bed rest (1 point), rather than strict bed confinement for over 72 hours, because he gets up with crutches for meals and hygiene.
- Previous ultrasound-confirmed popliteal DVT: 3 points, even though it was provoked and has resolved.
- Planned arthroscopic surgery: 2 points. It is not also scored as minor surgery.
Total under this bed-rest classification = 0 + 5 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 13.
Final answer: 13
